variants.title: Count work in flight
variants.context: Concurrency is the average number of requests inside a system. In a stable system, it equals completed requests per second multiplied by average end-to-end seconds.
variants.prompt: A stable service completes 200 requests/second. Mean time in the system is 0.25 seconds. How many requests are in flight on average?
variants.hint: Multiply throughput by average time in seconds.
variants.explanation: 200 × 0.25 = 50.0. The rate is per second, so the time in the system has to be in seconds too.

mistakes.feedback: That divides the rate by the time. Concurrency is 200 multiplied by 0.25.
That is the completion rate alone. The 0.25 second time in the system still has to be applied.

variants.title: Count work in flight
variants.context: Concurrency is the average number of requests inside a system. In a stable system, it equals completed requests per second multiplied by average end-to-end seconds.
variants.prompt: A stable service completes 80 requests/second. Mean time in the system is 1.5 seconds. How many requests are in flight on average?
variants.hint: Multiply throughput by average time in seconds.
variants.explanation: 80 × 1.5 = 120.0. The rate is per second, so keep the time at 1.5 seconds rather than 1,500 milliseconds.

mistakes.feedback: That multiplied by 1,500 milliseconds. Keep the time in seconds: 80 times 1.5.
That is the completion rate alone. The 1.5 second time in the system still has to be applied.

variants.title: Add a sequential path
variants.context: Sequential stages run one after another. Their elapsed times add when there is no overlap.
variants.prompt: A request spends 20 ms in the network, 30 ms in the service, and 50 ms in storage. The stages are sequential. What is total latency?
variants.explanation: 20 + 30 + 50 = 100 ms. More concurrent requests do not shorten this single path.

mistakes.feedback: That is the slowest stage. Sequential stages add, so 20 plus 30 plus 50.
That is the answer in seconds. The unit here is milliseconds.

variants.title: Choose the right target
variants.context: Latency measures how long one request takes. Throughput measures how many finish per second.
variants.prompt: Users wait 2 seconds for a response, but the service handles all incoming traffic. Which target addresses their complaint?
options: Increase throughput without changing response time.
variants.hint: Ask whether the symptom concerns time, volume, or waiting.
variants.explanation: The complaint concerns time per request, so measure and reduce the slow path.

variants.title: Choose the right target
variants.context: Latency measures how long one request takes. Throughput measures how many finish per second.
variants.prompt: A worker finishes one task in 10 ms but can run only one task at a time. Which change can increase aggregate throughput if tasks are independent?
options: Raise the per-task timeout to 50 ms.
Combine all tasks into a single serial worker.
Add workers while downstream has spare capacity.
variants.hint: Ask whether the symptom concerns time, volume, or waiting.
variants.explanation: Independent workers can finish more tasks per second; downstream limits still matter.
optionFeedback: Revisit the requirement in the scenario. A longer timeout lets one task run longer; it does not add a second worker.
Revisit the requirement in the scenario. One serial worker still finishes one task at a time, so the rate is unchanged.
Independent workers can finish more tasks per second; downstream limits still matter.

variants.title: Choose the right target
variants.context: Latency measures how long one request takes. Throughput measures how many finish per second.
variants.prompt: Throughput stays flat while queue length and response time rise. What should you investigate?
options: Whether the queue needs a larger maximum size.
Whether retries should run more frequently.
variants.hint: Ask whether the symptom concerns time, volume, or waiting.
variants.explanation: A growing queue means work arrives faster than it leaves over this interval.
optionFeedback: Revisit the requirement in the scenario. A larger queue stores more waiting work and lengthens the wait.
A growing queue means work arrives faster than it leaves over this interval.
Revisit the requirement in the scenario. More retries add arrivals to a system that is already behind.
